title: Analyzing postpartum patients' attitudes towards medication for weight management: a mixed-methods analysis.
abstract: Pregnancy and the postpartum period present unique stressors that can be barriers to weight loss efforts. The landscape of weight management is rapidly evolving, but without specific understanding or consideration of postpartum people's needs and attitudes towards newer pharmaceutical options (e.g., GLP-1 agonists). We aim to characterize postpartum people's perspectives on weight management interventions in the weeks to months following birth. This study assesses the attitudes of postpartum people with a BMI >30 kg/m2 towards weight management in the immediate postpartum period. This was a prospective, observational study leveraging mixed-methods techniques to extract the opinions and stances of postpartum people from a single institution with a BMI >30 kg/m2 via semi-structured interviews. A total of three focus groups and two one-on-one interviews were conducted. Thematic qualitative analysis was performed to identify emergent themes, followed by a sentiment analysis to quantitatively compare the emotive lexical context of each major theme. We qualitatively identified four major themes during the interviews: attitudes about medication ("Medication"), attitudes towards and experiences with weight fluctuation ("Weight"), tools for losing weight ("Tools"), and concerns about long-term health ("Concern"). Quantitatively, participant statements about "Tools" were the most positive, with polarity scores (0.33 ± 0.27), while sentences related to "Concern" were the most negative (polarity scores 0.02 ± 0.25). Terms representing the emotions "joy," "anticipation," and "trust" were notably overrepresented compared to other emotions in sentences categorized as discussing "Tools." These positive stances were reaffirmed in our qualitative review, though participants were skeptical regarding the implications of weight loss medications on breastfeeding. They also conveyed concern about short-term use of medications, favoring a sustainable multimodal approach. Overall, participants expressed overwhelmingly positive attitudes towards weight management interventions in the postpartum period, specifically in conjunction with other lifestyle adjustments and support from medical and familial outlets. In semi-structured interviews, postpartum participants with a BMI >30 kg/m2 favored a comprehensive plan for weight loss and management-including pharmacologic interventions and social supports or lifestyle alterations-starting in the weeks to months postpartum. Though they highlighted lingering concerns regarding safety and efficacy of pharmacologic interventions in this context, participants were open to integrating medications as one of many tools to optimize long-term cardiometabolic well-being.

title: Mā te kimi ka kite, Mā te kite ka mōhio, Mā te mōhio ka Mārama Seek and discover, discover and know, know and become enlightened.
journal: The Proceedings of the Nutrition Society
abstract: The 59th Annual Scientific Meeting of the Nutrition Society of New Zealand was held at Tūhura Otago Museum, Dunedin (26-28 November 2025) under the theme "Advancing Nutrition: Evidence, Translation, and Action", reflecting the imperative to translate nutrition science into equitable, culturally grounded policy and practice. Scientific sessions spanned sustainable food systems, best practice in research methods and reporting, data sovereignty, women's health, sports nutrition, Māori and Pacific health, mental wellbeing, chronic disease prevention and management, and nutrition across the lifespan. Plenary presentations addressed systems approaches to Pacific food environments and policy; Māori considerations for indigenous data sovereignty in administrative and health datasets; the CONSORT-Nut extension to strengthen reporting of nutrition randomised controlled trials; menopause and cardiometabolic health; regional action on non-communicable diseases (including the MANA monitoring framework); the benefits and risks of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists within a weight-inclusive, culturally responsive model of care; and critical appraisal of social media nutrition narratives affecting active women. The Muriel Bell Lecture, highlighted strengths-based Pacific nutrition initiatives informed by the Fonofale model of health. Workshops emphasised practical translation, including behaviour change, food waste reduction in aged residential care, weight-inclusive care for GLP-1 users, culinary nutrition, oral health, and dementia risk reduction. Overall, the conference showcased contemporary nutrition research and practice and underscored shared responsibility to turn evidence into action that improves population health and reduces inequities.

title: Treat-to-target weight management in fibromyalgia: a preliminary estimate of clinically meaningful weight loss.
Insights from multi-omics on GLP-1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
abstract: Glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the management of T2D and obesity. T2D clustering highlights distinct phenotypes that differ in GLP-1RA benefit. While they have markedly improved quality of life for many individuals, converging evidence indicates that genetic variation, metabolomic remodeling, and gut microbiota composition contribute to substantial inter-individual variability in GLP-1RA efficacy and tolerability. GLP-1RAs, in return, can variably affect the metabolome and microbiome composition in treated individuals. This review focuses on human multi-omics GLP-1RA intervention studies, complemented by relevant mechanistic preclinical evidence. Genetic variation in GLP1R, TCF7L2, and other loci has been associated with differences in glycaemic and weight outcomes, although most findings remain preliminary, inconsistent across populations, or not yet replicated. Pharmacometabolomic studies show recurrent of lipid-related pathways including, glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, ceramides, amino acids, and bile acids, with drug-specific signatures. GLP-1RAs are also associated with changes in gut microbial composition, including taxa such as Akkermansia and Bacteroides, although the direction and clinical significance of these changes vary across studies due to methodological and population heterogeneity. Multi-omics and AI-based models show promise for predicting treatment response by integrating genetic, metabolic, microbial, and clinical data to supporting more effective and individualized therapy and advancing precision medicine.

title: Precision Pharmacotherapy for Childhood Obesity: Molecular Targets Beyond Single GLP-1 Receptor Agonism and a Framework for Disease Modification.
abstract: Childhood obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease shaped by genetic susceptibility, neuroendocrine signaling, energy homeostasis, adipose dysfunction, insulin resistance, and environmental exposure. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have markedly improved treatment efficacy, but heterogeneous response, weight recurrence after withdrawal, residual organ risk, and limited long-term pediatric data expose the limitations of a single-pathway, weight-centered model. This narrative review integrates the molecular rationale and clinical evidence for precision pharmacotherapy beyond single GLP-1 receptor agonism. It examines glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 and GLP-1/glucagon co-agonism, triple agonism, amylin combinations, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) analogues, leptin replacement, and melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonism, separating established pediatric evidence from adult proof-of-concept and preclinical inference. Genotype-directed treatment for monogenic and syndromic obesity and lesion-directed treatment for acquired hypothalamic obesity provide the clearest examples of causal pathway correction. For common obesity, treatment selection should integrate developmental stage, hyperphagia, insulin resistance, ectopic fat, body composition, genetic context, treatment burden, and early response. Disease modification should be evaluated across growth, puberty, bone and lean tissue, beta cell and hepatic health, physical function, psychosocial well-being, safety, and durability. A dynamic cycle of phenotyping, mechanism-based treatment, multidomain monitoring, adaptation, and longitudinal re-phenotyping may improve the clinical relevance of pediatric obesity care.

title: The Gut Microbiota-Epigenome Axis in Bariatric Surgery: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Perspectives.
abstract: The global prevalence of obesity has reached an alarming level, placing a significant burden on public health systems and individual well-being. Bariatric surgeries (BSs) result in greater and more sustained weight reduction than emerging medications such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). Despite the proven effectiveness of BS, considerable inter-individual variability in postoperative outcomes persists, with differences in weight loss and remission of obesity-related comorbidities among patients. Gut microbiota gene richness has been shown to change following BS. Importantly, the influence of the gut microbiota extends beyond conventional metabolic pathways to include interactions with the host epigenome. Although growing evidence suggests that microbiota-derived metabolites can influence epigenetic processes, whether inter-individual differences in gut microbiota composition contribute to variability in postoperative weight loss and metabolic outcomes following BS remains largely unknown. The gut microbiota-epigenome axis represents a potential molecular interface between postoperative gastrointestinal remodeling and metabolic adaptation. Surgical remodeling of the gastrointestinal tract reshapes the gut microbiota and its metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and B vitamins, which may regulate host gene expression through histone deacetylase inhibition, DNA methylation, and modulation of systemic inflammation. Current evidence suggests that postoperative probiotic supplementation may improve glucose homeostasis, lipid profiles, and vitamin B12 and D status while having little or no additional effect on postoperative weight loss. Future research should address the limitations of existing studies by conducting adequately powered, high-quality randomized controlled trials integrating multi-omics technologies and precision medicine approaches to identify microbiome-based therapeutic targets, including postbiotic interventions. Further elucidation of this axis may support the development of precision bariatric strategies, although the clinical utility of microbiome- and epigenome-targeted interventions remains to be established.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Adolescents with Severe Obesity.
abstract: This commentary examines the role of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in adolescents with severe obesity, focusing on the intersection between metabolic benefit and mental health vulnerability. Recent trials demonstrate significant reductions in BMI and improvement in cardiometabolic outcomes among adolescents treated with GLP-1's, leading to inclusion in contemporary paediatric obesity guidelines. However, concerns remain regarding long-term psychological and neurodevelopmental effects, particularly as many clinical trials exclude young people with psychiatric comorbidity. Adolescents with obesity frequently experience anxiety, depression, weight stigma, disordered eating, and Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs), all of which may influence treatment engagement and outcomes. This article highlights the need for careful multidisciplinary assessment prior to initiating pharmacotherapy. We argue that prescribing decisions should extend beyond BMI alone and incorporate psychological wellbeing, eating disorder risk, social context, and family capacity to ensure safe, equitable, and developmentally appropriate obesity care.

title: The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists as a treatment for obesity in older people: risks and benefits.
journal: Current opinion in clinical nutrition and metabolic care
abstract: Obesity is an increasingly important health problem in older adults (≥65 years) and is associated with osteoarthritis, impaired mobility, reduced quality of life, cardiovascular disease, and other age-related comorbidities. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding the benefits and risks of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) therapy in older adults. GLP-1 RAs, initially developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), have emerged as effective pharmacological options for weight reduction and cardiovascular risk reduction. Studies suggest that GLP-1 RAs have clinically meaningful weight loss in older adults, with efficacy comparable to that observed in younger populations. In addition, selected GLP-1 RAs have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits, including reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), which may be particularly relevant in older individuals with a high burden of cardiovascular disease. Nevertheless, several concerns should be considered before treatment initiation, including gastrointestinal intolerance, sarcopenia-related muscle loss, ophthalmologic complications, and hypoglycaemia when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Furthermore, polypharmacy and age-related physiological changes may increase the likelihood of clinically relevant drug interactions. Current evidence indicates that GLP-1 RAs may represent a valuable therapeutic option for carefully selected older adults, particularly those with severe obesity and cardiometabolic comorbidities.

title: Pharmacological therapy and dietary intervention for obesity management: A one-year prospective cohort study in Baghdad.
journal: Journal of education and health promotion
abstract: Evidence directly comparing long-term pharmacological therapy and structured dietary intervention for obesity in Middle Eastern populations is limited. This study provides 12-month real-world comparative data from specialized obesity clinics in Baghdad, Iraq. A prospective cohort study included 120 adults with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2) from June 2024 to June 2025. Participants received either pharmacological therapy (orlistat 120 mg three times daily or liraglutide 3.0 mg/day; n = 60) with standard lifestyle advice, or intensive individualized dietary counseling by board-certified dietitians (n = 60). The primary outcome was percentage weight loss at 12 months. Secondary outcomes assessed body composition, metabolic parameters, physical activity, adherence, adverse effects, and quality of life. Between-group differences were analyzed using independent t-tests with exact P values and 95% confidence intervals. At 12 months, pharmacological therapy associated with greater early weight loss but reached a plateau (13.5 ± 3.7% vs. 11.3 ± 4.3%, P < 0.001; 95% CI: 1.1-2.8%). Dietary intervention associated with higher fat-mass loss (68.9% vs. 53.1%, P < 0.001), better lean-mass preservation (P = 0.003), and superior improvements in LDL-cholesterol (P = 0.012), fasting glucose (P = 0.047), systolic blood pressure (P = 0.041), and physical activity (P = 0.001). Adherence (73.3% vs. 58.3%, P = 0.038) and patient satisfaction (P < 0.001) were higher with diet, while gastrointestinal side effects were more common with pharmacotherapy (68.3% vs. 11.7%, P < 0.001). Intensive dietary counseling yielded to superior long-term metabolic, behavioral, and patient-centered outcomes with better adherence, supporting its use as a first-line obesity treatment. Pharmacological therapy may be an adjunct for selected patients, highlighting the importance of structured, dietitian-led lifestyle programs within health systems.

title: How Well Are We Measuring Nausea? A Narrative Review of Patient-Reported Outcome Gaps in GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Obesity Trials.
abstract: Across the full spectrum of major clinical trials evaluating glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for obesity management, nausea consistently emerges as the most documented adverse effect, yet the methods used to capture it have received little scrutiny relative to their clinical importance. This narrative review traces how nausea was actually measured across the pivotal liraglutide (SCALE), semaglutide (STEP) and tirzepatide (SURMOUNT) obesity trial programmes, and situates those methods against the standards set out in the Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) and the United States Food and Drug Administration's Patient-Focused Drug Development guidance. Across all three drug classes, nausea was ascertained through investigator-recorded, spontaneously reported adverse events coded to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), a pharmacovigilance framework built for a different purpose than symptom characterization, rather than through any validated, symptom-specific patient-reported outcome instrument. This observation gains further importance when considered alongside a second, less widely recognized fact: these same trial programmes devoted substantial methodological effort to developing and implementing a rigorous, quality of life measure specifically for obesity, the Impact of Weight on Quality of Life-Lite Clinical Trials Version in addition to the Short Form-36 and EuroQol-5D. We argue that this asymmetry, more than any single mismeasurement, helps explain why real-world persistence with these agents falls so far short of what trial-reported tolerability figures would predict, and we outline what a fit-for-purpose metabolic nausea instrument would need to capture that adverse-event surveillance cannot.

title: GLP-1 Ads Are Everywhere. What Are They Doing to Our Body Image?
abstract: GLP-1 medications are incredibly accessible-while this may be a net positive for eligible patients, their widespread marketing may not be. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Anna Zucker reports on concerns being raised about the potential impact of GLP-1 marketing practices on body image and well-being.

title: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years: A Review.
abstract: Obesity affects 15% of children aged 2 to 5 years and 22% of children aged 6 to 11 years in the US. Obesity in children is associated with dyslipidemia, hypertension, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnea. Compared with normal-weight peers, children with obesity have lower quality of life and are 5 times more likely to have obesity in adulthood. Body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) is used to identify children at risk for excess adiposity, and guidelines recommend that clinicians screen for obesity using BMI starting at age 2 years. Among children, obesity is defined using standardized age- and sex-specific growth charts, with obesity defined as BMI in the 95th or higher percentile and severe obesity as BMI of 120% or greater of the 95th percentile. Obesity treatment in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, consisting of at least 26 contact hours of face-to-face group or family-based activities that incorporate nutrition, physical activity, and behavior change education delivered to the child and caregivers over a 3- to 12-month period. Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment reduces BMI by 0.7 compared with children who do not participate in intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment. The only obesity pharmacotherapy currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for children younger than 12 years is setmelanotide, a melanocortin-4 receptor agonist, which is indicated for 3 forms of rare monogenic obesity (LEPR, POMC, and PCSK1 genetic variants), Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and acquired hypothalamic obesity. Liraglutide is currently only FDA approved for youth aged 12 years or older; however, a randomized clinical trial among children aged 6 to younger than 12 years demonstrated that, compared with placebo, liraglutide reduced BMI by 7.4%. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is rarely used in children younger than age 12 years and evidence supporting its use in children is limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood. Obesity in children is associated with chronic disease, such as hypertension, and with poor quality of life. Evidence-based treatment for obesity in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, and pharmacotherapy may provide additional benefit, although short- and long-term safety and efficacy data are limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.

title: Dose-response profiles in incretin and multi-agonist obesity pharmacotherapy.
journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology
abstract: Incretin and multi-agonist therapies have transformed obesity pharmacotherapy, but dose selection remains less mature than efficacy assessment. This critical narrative review examines nonlinear relationships among administered dose, systemic exposure, weight and cardiometabolic benefit, gastrointestinal tolerability, treatment persistence, and maintenance. Across established and newer programs, average efficacy generally increases with dose, yet incremental gains may narrow at higher exposure while adverse-event burden and discontinuation can increase. The maturity of evidence is heterogeneous, and later-stage programs should not be interpreted as clinically equivalent to agents supported mainly by earlier-phase dose-ranging data. Moreover, an "optimal dose" is not an endpoint-independent quantity: the exposure most appropriate for weight loss may differ from that relevant to glycemic control, cardiovascular benefit, body composition, tolerability, or maintenance. We therefore distinguish nominal dose from exposure and present response-guided titration as a hypothesis-generating framework for prospective testing, not as an evidence-based dosing algorithm. Existing continuation and withdrawal studies support the importance of ongoing pharmacological treatment after successful weight loss but do not establish a minimum or optimal de-intensified maintenance dose. Future trials should jointly model efficacy, safety, body composition, patient-reported outcomes, pharmacokinetics, and discontinuation to test objective-specific, patient-level dosing strategies.

title: Patient-Reported Outcomes Following Initiation or Simplification of Treatment With iGlarLixi in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Given the significant burden that diabetes self-management poses, it is important to assess patient-reported outcomes (PROs) for Type 2 diabetes (T2D) treatments in clinical trials and real-world studies. Complex insulin regimens are associated with increased risk of hypoglycaemia and body weight gain, which could negatively impact treatment adherence and, therefore, achievement of glycaemic targets. iGlarLixi is a once-daily fixed-ratio combination of insulin glargine 100 U/mL and the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), lixisenatide. iGlarLixi is an effective treatment alternative to complex insulin regimens, with a favourable between-group difference in body weight and reduced risk of hypoglycaemia. This is the first review to summarise data from multiple validated PRO measures for recent iGlarLixi studies (Soli-CGM, SoliMix, Soli-SWITCH, IDEAL, SUCCESS and SIMPLIFY JP), including: Global Treatment Effectiveness Evaluation, Audit of Diabetes Dependent Quality of Life, Diabetes Medication Satisfaction Tool, Diabetes Therapy-Related Quality of Life, Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, Hypoglycaemic Attitudes and Behaviour Scale and Treatment-Related Impact Measure Diabetes. In clinical studies, once-daily iGlarLixi was associated with numerical improvements in selected treatment satisfaction measures in those who switched from: complex insulin regimens (once- or twice-daily premixed insulin and basal-bolus insulin), basal insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications. Additionally, in real-world studies, iGlarLixi was generally associated with improvements in treatment satisfaction and quality of life outcomes in adults with T2D who previously received basal-bolus insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications ± basal insulin or GLP-1 RAs. In conclusion, a once-daily injection of iGlarLixi may offer a clinically beneficial, simplified treatment option for adults with T2D compared with complex insulin-based regimens.

title: Modern Obesity Treatment: Efficacy, Safety, and Future Directions of GLP-1 (Glucagon-Like Peptide-1) and GIP (Glucose-Dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide) Receptor Agonists.
abstract: Obesity is a chronic and heterogeneous disease associated with a substantial burden of metabolic, cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal complications. In recent years, incretin-based therapies have changed the pharmacological management of obesity by providing levels of weight reduction that were previously difficult to achieve with medical treatment alone. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the efficacy, safety, and broader clinical effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with overweight or obesity. Relevant literature was identified through searches of major medical databases, with emphasis on randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, clinical guidelines, and pivotal phase 2 and phase 3 trials. Liraglutide established the role of GLP-1 receptor agonism in weight management, while semaglutide provided greater and more sustained weight reduction. Tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, produced greater weight loss than semaglutide in direct comparative studies. Beyond weight reduction, incretin-based therapies have demonstrated favorable effects on glycemic control, cardiovascular risk, kidney outcomes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and quality of life. Gastrointestinal adverse effects, particularly nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, remain the most common limitations and are most prominent during dose escalation. Emerging multi-receptor and combination therapies, including retatrutide, CagriSema, MariTide, and amycretin, may further expand treatment options, although long-term efficacy and safety data remain limited. Overall, incretin-based therapies support a shift from weight-centered obesity treatment toward individualized, complication-oriented long-term care.

title: Advances in disease management and treatment outcomes for obesity and knee osteoarthritis in primary care practice.
abstract: The lifetime risk of developing knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is approximately doubled in people with obesity compared with those without obesity. Many patients with KOA are treated by primary care physicians in the community setting. We performed a targeted literature search on PubMed to identify relevant literature describing the impact of weight loss in patients with obesity and KOA. A strong body of evidence supports the use of weight loss through lifestyle interventions, including caloric restriction in combination with exercise, as a primary intervention in patients with KOA and obesity. Studies show that these interventions are associated with improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life; however, adherence to lifestyle interventions can be challenging, even with individually tailored programs. Obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, are emerging as a new addition to weight management approaches in KOA, with a recent phase 3 clinical study demonstrating the benefits of semaglutide for weight loss in adults with KOA and high body mass index. Although initial data are promising, further clinical evidence is required, and perceived barriers to use need to be addressed before obesity medications can be widely adopted into clinical practice for patients with KOA. Specifically, further data are required to guide decisions regarding optimal treatment duration with obesity medications and to establish their tolerability profile associated with longer-term use. The importance of preserving functional muscle mass in patients with KOA and mitigation of weight regain after obesity medication treatment withdrawal are also identified as areas warranting further research. In this narrative review, we provide practical recommendations to primary care physicians on integrating obesity medications into weight-loss programs, including patient screening, risk stratification, communication, use of guidelines, and the benefits of a multidisciplinary approach.

title: Outcomes in patients with diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and heart failure treated with tirzepatide or dulaglutide: SURPASS-CVOT analysis.
abstract: The impact of tirzepatide and dulaglutide on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and heart failure (HF) outcomes according to HF status is unknown. Patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were treated with tirzepatide up to 15 mg or dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly (average 4 years). The incidence of MACE-3 [cardiovascular (CV) death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke], MACE-4 (CV death, MI, stroke, coronary revascularization) and composite of all-cause or CV death and hospitalization or urgent visits for HF were analysed in patients with and without a history of HF. A history of HF (20.3%) was associated with more coronary artery disease and prior MI. Incidences of event categories were higher in the HF group. The hazard ratio (HR) for all-cause death or hospitalization or urgent visits for HF on tirzepatide vs. dulaglutide was 0.83 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.70-0.99] in patients with HF and 0.88 (95%CI 0.78-1.00) without HF. The HR for CV death or hospitalization or urgent visits for HF was 0.85 (95%CI 0.70-1.03) and 0.96 (95%CI 0.83-1.12), for MACE-3 0.90 (95%CI 0.76-1.08) and 0.93 (95%CI 0.83-1.04), and for MACE-4 0.81 (95%CI 0.69-0.95) and 0.91 (95%CI 0.83-1.00) in patients with and without HF, respectively. The patient-reported outcomes of APPADL and EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scores improved and were higher on tirzepatide in both groups. With overall non-inferiority established, this exploratory analysis revealed lower rates of the composite of all-cause death or HF events, or MACE-4 among patients with T2D and HF treated with tirzepatide compared with dulaglutide.

title: The pharmacotherapy for pediatric obesity: insights and challenges from adult weight-loss medications.
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: Obesity significantly increases the risk of developing other chronic diseases and shortens the life expectancy by 5 to 8 years. Childhood obesity is particularly prominent as 80% of teenagers with obesity have shown it to persist into adulthood. With reference to the development of adult medication, the present review summarises the recent research progress in the development of pediatric anti-obesity drugs. The current management guidelines support the use of medication for adolescents aged 12 and above when lifestyle measures are ineffective. Early weight-loss drugs like the serotonergic agonist fenfluramine and the norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor sibutramine were withdrawn due to severe safety issues. Rainbow pills and the CB1 inhibitor rimonabant also failed over neuropsychiatric toxicity. These highlighted inadequate safety profiling in initial development, and there were almost no studies on children. Recently, GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as semaglutide, and the dual-target agonist tirzepatide have gained popularity among adults and adolescents with obesity. However, it still faces significant limitations, including the long-term neurodevelopmental safety of adolescents, high costs and limited insurance coverage, and widespread gastrointestinal side effects. It is foreseeable that the focus of adult weight loss medication research may gradually shift to multi-target new drugs, including the dual agonist mazdutide and the triple receptor agonist retatrutide. Therefore, the development of pediatric weight loss drugs should also focus on the GLP-1 receptor agonists and multi-target new drugs. In addition, there is an urgent need to verify the safety and efficacy of approved weight loss medications through pediatric clinical trials.

title: Advances in pharmacologic management of obesity: oral semaglutide for weight management.
abstract: Obesity is a chronic, multifactorial disease characterized by excessive adiposity and associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and reduced quality of life. Despite the widespread adoption of lifestyle interventions, long-term weight maintenance remains challenging, highlighting the need for effective pharmacologic therapies. Recent advances, including the US Food and Drug Administration approval of oral semaglutide, offer new opportunities for patient-centered obesity management. Evidence from the OASIS 1 and OASIS 4 trials demonstrates that oral semaglutide, combined with lifestyle intervention, produces clinically meaningful weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity without type 2 diabetes, while improving physical function and cardiometabolic risk markers, such as waist circumference, lipids, and inflammatory parameters. These trials further underscore the benefits of an oral formulation in improving accessibility and adherence compared with injectable therapies. Collectively, oral semaglutide represents a significant advancement in obesity pharmacotherapy, complementing lifestyle interventions and providing both metabolic and functional benefits. Future studies addressing long-term efficacy, cardiovascular outcomes, comparative effectiveness with other agents, and real-world implementation will be essential to fully define its role in comprehensive, individualized obesity care.

title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.

title: From PCOS to PMOS: reframing the clinical pathway around insulin sensitivity and weight-neutral metabolic risk.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous condition associated with reproductive, metabolic, pregnancy, and psychological morbidity across the life course. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) was recently proposed through a multistep global consensus process, with implementation across guidelines and health systems still under way. This Perspective argues that the clinical value of the naming proposal will depend on whether it redirects care beyond ovarian morphology and body size. Insulin resistance can serve as an actionable management hub linking reproductive endocrine dysfunction with longer-term metabolic risk in a substantial subgroup, but it is neither universal, the sole cause of the syndrome, nor a diagnostic criterion. Routine fasting insulin measurement or homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance should therefore not be introduced as diagnostic requirements. Instead, we propose a weight-neutral, insulin-sensitivity-centered, life-course pathway aligned with existing guideline recommendations. Glycemic status, lipids, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, pregnancy planning, psychological health, and risk-directed liver assessment should be considered according to clinical guidance without using BMI as an exclusion criterion. Lifestyle intervention should be evaluated through metabolic, functional, reproductive, and quality-of-life outcomes, not weight change alone. Metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists should remain confined to guideline-supported indications and evidence limitations. Whether PMOS improves risk recognition, guideline adherence, patient experience, or continuity of care remains to be established.

title: Exercise, Nutrition and GLP-1 Medicines to Improve Body Weight and Muscle Function in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction.
abstract: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on lifestyle, pharmacological, surgical, and multimodal interventions targeting muscle strength, body composition, and functional capacity in HFpEF with sarcopenia and/or obesity. Exercise, particularly concurrent endurance and resistance training protocols, improve aerobic capacity, functional performance, symptoms, and quality of life in HFpEF. Protein supplementation may preserve muscle mass, while caloric restriction may enhance aerobic capacity and function butdecreases muscle mass. SGLT2i and GLP-1 medicines may reduce hospitalizations and improve symptoms, with GLP-1 medicines producing greater weight loss and performance benefits. Bariatric surgery may also achieve substantial weight loss and functional improvements, although evidence in HFpEF with obesity is limited. Obesity-related HFpEF may benefit from a combination of resistance exercise and adequate protein intake to preserve muscle during weight loss, while pharmacotherapy can be used to support cardiac function. Future trials should evaluate multimodal interventions to mitigate frailty risk in HFpEF.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in perimenopause and early postmenopause: clinical role, cardiometabolic benefits and knowledge gaps.
journal: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society
abstract: Perimenopause and early postmenopause represent a critical metabolic transition with adverse changes in body composition, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism and cardiometabolic health, contributing to increased rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. As the prevalence of obesity continues to rise among midlife women, effective therapeutic strategies are increasingly needed. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have emerged as highly effective treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes through their effects on appetite regulation, weight reduction, glucose homeostasis and metabolic health. Beyond their established role, GLP-1 RAs have demonstrated favorable effects on visceral adiposity, glycemic control, lipid profiles, hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular outcomes. Preliminary experimental evidence also suggests possible complementary effects when combined with menopausal hormone therapy (MHT). However, menopause-specific evidence remains limited. This review summarizes the current evidence regarding the efficacy, safety and clinical application of GLP-1 RAs in perimenopausal and early postmenopausal women. Particular attention is given to their effects on cardiometabolic health, cardiovascular risk, bone and muscle health, cancer risk, cognition and potential interactions with MHT. Although GLP-1 RAs represent a promising therapeutic option for obesity and metabolic dysfunction during menopause, important knowledge gaps remain regarding their long-term safety, effects on menopause-related outcomes and optimal integration into comprehensive menopausal care. The efficacy, safety and potential interactions of GLP-1 RAs when used in combination with MHT remain to be determined.

title: The Gut-Brain Axis in Parkinson's Disease: From Clinical Observation toward Mechanism-Based Precision Medicine.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Gastrointestinal dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), affecting quality of life, nutrition, medication response, and potentially the earliest stages of pathogenesis. This perspective traces the evolution of the gut from a neglected source of non-motor symptoms to a central component of biological models of PD. Gastrointestinal manifestations are physiologically heterogeneous and require objective phenotyping to distinguish dysphagia, gastroparesis, slow transit, defecatory dysfunction, and overlapping mechanisms. The body-first/brain-first framework further suggests that Lewy pathology may follow distinct anatomical trajectories, with early enteric and autonomic involvement defining a subgroup in which gut-directed biomarkers and therapies may be especially relevant. Alterations of the gut microbiome are reproducibly associated with PD, although geography, constipation, medication, diet, disease stage, and reverse causation complicate interpretation. Emerging work is shifting from taxonomy toward microbial functions and host pathways, including barrier integrity, immune and enteroendocrine signaling, short-chain fatty acids, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), host genetic susceptibility, α-synuclein aggregation and propagation, and microbial levodopa metabolism. Trials of probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, and dietary interventions remain heterogeneous and have not established disease-modifying efficacy. Progress will require longitudinal studies in prodromal and subtype-defined populations, objective gastrointestinal measurements, integrated microbial, host-genetic and other multi-omics, mechanistic human and animal models, and clinical trials combining target-engagement markers with meaningful outcomes. Such an approach may enable precision gut-brain medicine for appropriately selected patients with PD. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Tirzepatide and Glucagon-like Peptide-1/Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide Therapy: Quality of Life, Filipino Diet Culture, and Safe Access.
Individualized Treatment Approaches for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Older Adults: Beyond Continuous Positive Airway Pressure.
journal: Advances in geriatric medicine and research
abstract: With an aging population and greater prevalence of metabolic disorders, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is increasingly observed in older patients. OSA in older adults often occurs in the setting of various comorbidities, such as cognitive, cardiac, and metabolic dysfunction, placing these patients at greater risk. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the first-line treatment for OSA in most patients, but adherence with CPAP decreases with increasing age. Current literature on considerations and efficacy of treatment modalities for OSA in older patients is limited. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on CPAP and non-CPAP therapies of OSA in older adults with particular attention to age-specific differences in clinical presentation, diagnostic challenges, and implications for quality of life. Relevant guidelines, clinical studies, and systematic reviews selected from the PubMed and Cochrane databases through April 2026 were summarized and categorized based on type of therapy. Some non-CPAP alternatives appear promising or effective in selected adults for improving metrics of sleep, quality of life, and mitigating comorbidities, but for geriatric-specific comparative evidence remains limited, indirect, observational, or derived from adults substantially younger than the target population. Lifestyle modifications, positional therapy, and oral appliances may yield benefits in older patients comparable to those seen in their younger counterparts, but age-stratified studies are limited. While pharmacotherapy is an area of emerging study, GLP-1 RAs show significant early potential with multifaceted benefits, although supporting studies have been primarily conducted in middle-aged adults. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation has emerged as a prominent OSA treatment alternative with improved adherence compared to CPAP in in small elderly-specific studies. OSA management in older patients is highly nuanced with multifactorial consideration of polypharmacy, comorbidities, and patient preferences to optimize patient outcomes. Larger-scale, prospective studies specific to older patients are warranted to assess treatment efficacy, adherence, and adverse effects in this population.

title: Incretin-Based Therapy in Patients with Malignancy and Obesity or Type 2 Diabetes. An Italian Association of Medical Oncology (AIOM), Italian Association of Medical Diabetologists (AMD), Italian Society of Diabetology (SID), Italian Society of Endocrinology (SIE), Italian Society of Pharmacology (SIF), and Italian Society of Obesity (SIO) Position Paper.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have emerged as pivotal agents in the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity, with well-established metabolic and cardiovascular benefits that translate into improvement in quality of life and life expectancy. While a potential benefit may also be hypothesized in patients with metabolic disorders and malignancy, robust clinical evidence is still lacking. In recent years, attention has turned to their potential impact on cancer risk, although current evidence remains limited and, in some cases, conflicting. Several biological pathways, such as improvements in insulin sensitivity, reductions in chronic inflammation, modulation of cellular signaling, and changes in the tumor microenvironment, have been proposed as possible mechanisms through which GLP-1RAs might influence cancer development or progression. However, available data derive from preclinical or observational studies, and high-quality prospective clinical evidence is still lacking. While some reports suggest possible protective associations in specific cancer types, others raise concerns about potential risks, particularly in hormonally sensitive or receptor-expressing tissues. This position paper synthesizes available data on the oncologic safety and potential antitumor effects of GLP-1RAs, highlights key knowledge gaps, and discusses clinical implications, underscoring the need for further research to clarify their role in cancer prevention and treatment.

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in psoriasis management.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic, systemic inflammatory skin disease associated with musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, metabolic, psychiatric, and gastrointestinal comorbidities. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists have emerged as potential therapeutic adjuncts for psoriasis because, beyond their metabolic effects, these agents exhibit anti-inflammatory properties and may reduce cytokine expression and inflammatory biomarkers. This review summarizes current evidence from randomized trials and nonrandomized studies on GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with psoriasis and discusses their potential role in disease management. Observational studies of liraglutide, semaglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide generally showed improvements in psoriasis severity, body weight, metabolic parameters, inflammatory biomarkers, and quality of life, although most studies were limited by small sample sizes and uncontrolled designs. Randomized trials likewise suggest dermatologic benefit, particularly in patients with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, or both. Most notably, the phase 3b TOGETHER trial demonstrated greater skin clearance and weight reduction with ixekizumab plus tirzepatide than with ixekizumab alone in patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and overweight or obesity. Complementary findings from the TOGETHER-Psoriatic Arthritis trial showed improvement in psoriatic arthritis disease activity as early as week four, before clinically meaningful weight loss, supporting the potential weight-independent anti-inflammatory effects of these agents. Future studies should include patients without obesity or diabetes to clarify the relative contributions of weight loss and direct anti-inflammatory effects to clinical response and determine whether the dermatologic benefits of GLP-1-based therapies extend to patients without underlying metabolic dysfunction.

title: Real-world effectiveness and safety of low-dose tirzepatide in Japanese people with type 2 diabetes: a multicenter, retrospective, single-arm, observational study-East Shizuoka Tirzepatide (ESTATE) study.
abstract: The glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist tirzepatide is available clinically. Although real-world studies of tirzepatide in Japanese people with type 2 diabetes (T2D) have been reported, data regarding low-dose tirzepatide and patient-reported outcomes in routine clinical practice remain limited. In this multicenter retrospective observational study, we evaluated changes in glycemic control, body mass index (BMI), metabolic parameters, patient-reported outcomes, and adverse events after initiation of low-dose tirzepatide in Japanese people with T2D. Eighty-eight subjects with T2D treated with an average dose of tirzepatide of 4.5 ± 1.0 mg/week for 24 weeks were retrospectively analyzed. The primary outcomes were changes in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and BMI from baseline to 24 weeks. HbA1c levels and BMI decreased over 24 weeks after initiation of low-dose tirzepatide (HbA1c, -1.5%; BMI, -1.5 kg/m2; both p < 0.001). Additionally, serum albumin was increased, and alanine transaminase and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were decreased significantly. In multivariable regression analysis, higher baseline HbA1c was associated with greater HbA1c reduction. In exploratory cross-sectional analyses, post-treatment Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire (DTSQ) scores were associated with higher baseline HbA1c, and Kanden Institute Stigma Scale (KISS) scores were associated with higher baseline BMI. Major adverse events linked with tirzepatide were gastrointestinal symptoms. In this multicenter retrospective single-arm observational study, HbA1c and BMI decreased over 24 weeks after low-dose tirzepatide initiation in Japanese people with T2D. These findings suggest that low-dose tirzepatide may be a useful treatment option in selected patients in routine clinical practice, although causal inference is limited by the observational design and lack of a control group.Trial Registration: National University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN Clinical Trial Registry, UMIN000053671; approval date: March 1, 2024).

title: Recent Studies on the Effectiveness and Safety of Anti-Obesity Medications: A Scoping Review.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Obesity remains a major global public health challenge associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and reduced quality of life, necessitating effective treatment strategies beyond lifestyle modifications. The present scoping review aimed to synthesize recent evidence on the effectiveness and safety of anti-obesity medications (AOMs). A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus in May 2025 to identify original studies published within the previous five years involving individuals with overweight or obesity receiving pharmacological interventions. A total of 42 articles representing 41 unique studies, predominantly randomized controlled trials (RCTs), were included in the evidence synthesis. The review encompassed glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), including semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, and orforglipron; multi-receptor incretin agonists, including tirzepatide, retatrutide, and survodutide; amylin-based combination therapy (cagrilintide plus semaglutide); established non-incretin AOMs (orlistat, phentermine, phentermine/topiramate, and naltrexone/bupropion); microbiome-targeted therapies; and nutraceutical-based interventions. Among these, GLP-1 RA consistently demonstrated substantial weight-loss efficacy, with semaglutide achieving approximately 10-16% weight loss, while tirzepatide produced approximately 15-21% weight reduction over treatment durations of 20-70 weeks. Emerging multi-receptor incretin agonists also demonstrated promising efficacy, whereas established non-incretin AOMs, microbiome-targeted therapies, and nutraceutical-based interventions generally produced modest or more heterogeneous outcomes. Gastrointestinal adverse events (AEs) were the most frequently reported across incretin-based therapies. Overall, incretin-based therapies currently provide the greatest weight-loss benefit, although evidence for several emerging pharmacotherapies, microbiome-targeted therapies, and nutraceutical-based interventions remains limited. Further well-designed comparative trials, mechanistic studies, and long-term real-world investigations are needed to better establish the durability, safety, and clinical applicability of emerging AOMs.

title: Estimating the Wider Societal Impact of Semaglutide Across Multiple Indications in Canada: An Economic Evaluation.
journal: Value in health : the journal of the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research
abstract: Medical treatments may have individual, healthcare, and societal impacts across multiple indications. Assessing the impact is challenging because of a focus on individual-level and indication-specific costs and benefits using narrow healthcare perspectives. A multiindication model was developed for Canada to evaluate the wider societal impacts of semaglutide. A population-level analysis estimated the 5-year (2025-2029) impact of semaglutide in a hypothetical population of 1 000 000 eligible treated Canadians with type 2 diabetes (T2D), cardiovascular (CV) disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and/or chronic kidney disease. Baseline prevalence and overlaps were estimated from published data. Treatment effects were derived from clinical trial comparisons of semaglutide versus standard care. Healthcare resource use reduction and cost-converted environmental impact were calculated from prevalence differences in control and treatment groups. Productivity was quantified using a US-based quality-of-life-driven model. Among treated individuals, 50% had 1 condition, 27% had 2, and 23% had ≥3 at baseline. Model analysis projected that there would be up to 235 000 fewer obesity cases and prevented 650 T2D cases, 8400 CV events, 1100 CV deaths, 5300 metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis stage 3-4 cases, 2200 stage 4 chronic kidney disease/end-stage renal disease cases, and 48 800 obesity- and T2D-related complications by 2029, although 21 200 gastrointestinal adverse events were estimated to occur. Treatment with semaglutide was estimated to avoid 22 200 hospitalizations and 330 kilotons of carbon dioxide equivalent, with estimated healthcare resource use cost reductions of CAD 2.0 billion and modeled productivity gains of CAD 19.9 billion, offsetting CAD 20.4 billion semaglutide (1 mg, 2.4 mg) treatment costs. Results were most sensitive to baseline utility values. Modeled 5-year impacts of semaglutide treatment suggest potential wide-ranging individual, healthcare, and societal benefits across cardiometabolic comorbidities that are not captured in traditional narrow healthcare perspectives.

title: Losing Muscle or Restoring Physiology? Reframing the Incretin Therapy Sarcopenia Concern.
abstract: The introduction of highly effective incretin-based therapies has transformed obesity management by achieving weight loss previously attainable mainly with bariatric surgery. However, the accompanying reduction in lean body mass has raised concerns regarding treatment-induced sarcopenia, particularly among older adults and other vulnerable populations. In this perspective, we argue that interpreting lean mass loss in isolation may be misleading. Current evidence indicates that approximately one-quarter to one-third of total weight loss consists of lean mass, a proportion comparable to that observed with other effective weight-loss interventions and consistent with physiological body composition remodeling rather than pathological muscle loss. Importantly, incretin therapies preferentially reduce fat mass, improve the lean-to-fat mass ratio, and are associated with improvements in physical function, mobility, and health-related quality of life. These observations challenge the assumption that reductions in lean body mass necessarily translate into clinically meaningful sarcopenia. Nevertheless, skeletal muscle health deserves particular attention in older adults and individuals with pre-existing sarcopenia, frailty, chronic kidney or cardiovascular disease, chronic inflammatory conditions, or poor nutritional status. In these populations, routine assessment of muscle strength and physical performance, together with adequate protein intake and structured resistance exercise, should complement pharmacological obesity treatment. Future research should prioritize muscle quality and function rather than lean mass alone to better define the clinical significance of body composition changes during incretin therapy.

title: Hypothalamic obesity in pediatric vs. adult craniopharyngioma: mechanisms, management, and cardiometabolic outcomes.
abstract: Hypothalamic obesity (HO) is a treatment-related complication in craniopharyngioma (CP) survivors that markedly impairs long-term health and quality of life. Although overall survival exceeds 90% for both pediatric and adult CP, HO prevalence and clinical course differ substantially by age at onset. We aimed to compare HO manifestations, mechanisms, and treatment response between pediatric and adult CP cohorts. We conducted a scoping review of studies published between 2000 and 2025, comparing pediatric (childhood-onset) versus adult-onset CP cohorts, classified by age at diagnosis. Data on obesity prevalence, mechanistic pathways, therapeutic interventions, and cardiometabolic outcomes were extracted and synthesized. In pediatric CP survivors, obesity rates rise from 5.7% pre-treatment to 57% post-treatment; in adults, from 19.2% to 29.2%. HO severity correlates with the extent of hypothalamic damage by Puget and QST grading. Key mechanisms include disrupted melanocortin signaling, central leptin and insulin resistance, and neuroinflammation via resistin-TLR4 and NLRP3 pathways. GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, semaglutide) have produced marked weight loss in small case series (up to 17% over 6 months with semaglutide), but randomized trials did not meet their primary weight outcomes and direct pediatric-versus-adult comparisons are lacking. Bariatric procedures yield moderate success; sleeve gastrectomy achieves 5-year weight loss comparable to that in non-CP controls (21.7% vs. 21.8%), whereas Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is less effective than in controls (22.7% vs. 32.0%). Both cohorts face significant long-term risks: 2.2-fold higher all-cause mortality and 9.3-fold higher diabetes risk in adults, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in 47% of pediatric survivors, metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease in 67.4% of adults, and insulin resistance in approximately 30% of pediatric patients. HO following CP shows distinct age-dependent trajectories in prevalence, underlying mechanisms, and clinical course; suggested age-related differences in treatment response remain to be confirmed in direct comparative studies. Tailored management integrating mechanistic insights and age-specific therapies is critical to mitigating the cardiometabolic burden in these patients.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis with Phenotype-Specific Effects and Dual Analytical Frameworks.
abstract: Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce cardiovascular risk in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D), evidence in heart failure (HF) has expanded across diverse trial populations and HF phenotypes but remains fragmented. We therefore performed an integrated systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of GLP-1 RAs across the spectrum of HF using complementary trial-level and phenotype-based analyses. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies published from inception to August 10, 2025. To provide an integrated assessment across heterogeneous HF populations, treatment effects were evaluated using dual analytical frameworks: trial-level analyses according to study design (dedicated HF with preserved ejection fraction [HFpEF] trials, HF with reduced ejection fraction [HFrEF] trials, and HF subgroups from cardiovascular outcome trials [CVOTs]) and phenotype-based analyses according to left ventricular ejection fraction (HFpEF vs HFrEF using a pragmatic threshold of 40%). A prespecified targeted analysis was conducted to specifically assess the efficacy of semaglutide. The primary outcomes were major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and the secondary outcomes included hospitalization for HF (HHF), the composite of cardiovascular death or any worsening HF events, cardiovascular death alone, and all-cause mortality. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random‑effects models. This meta-analysis included 14 trials, with a pooled total of 15,882 patients with HF. In phenotype‑based analyses for HFpEF, GLP‑1 RAs significantly reduced MACE (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66-0.94; p = 0.010), HHF (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.27-0.85; p = 0.012), the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF (HR 0.57; 95% CI 0.37-0.89; p = 0.013), and all‑cause mortality (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.62-0.89; p = 0.001). In contrast, in HFrEF, no significant reductions were observed for HHF, the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF, all-cause mortality, or MACE, although a reduction in cardiovascular death was noted (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.54-0.95; p = 0.019). Trial-level analyses showed that cardiovascular benefits were primarily observed in HF subgroups from CVOTs, including reductions in MACE (HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.73-0.92; p = 0.001), cardiovascular death (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.77-1.00; p = 0.05) and myocardial infarction (MI)/non-fatal MI (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.70-1.00; p = 0.046). Semaglutide showed benefits in HHF and the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF events predominantly among overweight or obese patients with HFpEF. GLP-1 RAs also improved functional capacity and quality of life in HFpEF. GLP-1 RAs were associated with favorable cardiovascular and HF-related outcomes in HFpEF, predominantly among overweight or obese individuals, whereas evidence of benefit in HFrEF remains limited. In trial-level analyses, benefits were primarily observed for atherosclerotic endpoints in HF subgroups from CVOTs. By integrating evidence, this study provides a unified overview of the effects of GLP-1 RAs across the spectrum of HF and supports further phenotype-specific randomized trials, particularly dedicated studies in HFrEF. Protocol registration PROSPERO (CRD420251079970).

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in hidradenitis suppurativa: A narrative review of emerging evidence.
abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by painful nodules, abscesses, and draining tunnels involving intertriginous areas. It frequently occurs alongside disorders of metabolic dysfunction including obesity, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome. HS places a substantial quality-of-life burden on its patients. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs), widely used for the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity, have emerged as promising candidates in managing HS. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the metabolic basis of HS and evaluates the role of GLP-1 RAs as adjunctive therapy. Collectively, these studies report improvements in disease activity measures as well as quality-of-life indices and health care utilization. Database analyses demonstrate associations with fewer cardiovascular events and improved extracutaneous outcomes. To date, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated GLP-1 RAs in HS. Current evidence is limited to observational studies, uncontrolled trials, and case reports. Concomitant treatments, lack of control groups, and selection bias limit causal inference. Although findings suggest there is proof of concept for GLP-1 RA therapy in HS, rigorous randomized controlled trials with standardized efficacy measures and adequate sample sizes are essential to establish clinical efficacy and define the role of GLP-1 RAs in the management of HS.

title: Molecular insights into GLP-1 receptor agonists and emerging metabolic-inflammatory targets in hidradenitis suppurativa.
abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is increasingly recognized as a systemic immunometabolic disease associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome (MetS). A metabolically unhealthy lean phenotype indicates that metabolic dysfunction and chronic low-grade inflammation may occur independently of increased body mass index (BMI) in patients with HS. Reduced effectiveness of biologic therapies in patients with obesity further supports targeting the upstream metabolic drivers of inflammation. This review outlines metabolic-inflammatory pathways proposed to contribute to HS, including insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) signaling, mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) overactivation, adipokine dysregulation, and gut-skin interactions. Building on this framework, this review evaluates evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dual incretin agonists, and other metabolic interventions, including metformin is evaluated. GLP-1RAs may serve as adjunctive metabolic therapies for selected patients with HS and obesity or MetS. By promoting weight loss and metabolic improvement, they may reduce systemic inflammation, perioperative risk, and improve responses to weight-based biologics. However, current evidence remains mainly observational and is confounded by concomitant therapies. Randomized controlled trials using well-defined dermatological and metabolic endpoints are needed before routine implementation.

title: Patient characteristics and early experiences with anti-obesity medications: the CAMP study.
abstract: The widespread adoption of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RAs) and related anti-obesity medications has transformed obesity treatment. However, limited data are available regarding the characteristics of patients receiving prescriptions for these medications and patients' real-world experiences with medication access, utilization, and supportive care. The CAMP (Characteristics of Anti-Obesity Medication Patients) study was conducted in a large academic health system. Phase I characterized demographic, clinical, and social determinants of health among adults prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide for weight management between July 2023 and June 2024. Phase II was an online survey assessing prescription fulfillment, medication use, payment methods, discontinuation, counseling, and referrals to additional services. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analyses were used to summarize findings and examine differences between patients receiving a prescription for the lowest dose versus the higher doses. A total of 21,610 adults prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide were identified through electronic health records in Phase I, and 2,628 completed the Phase II patient survey. Patients in Phase I were predominantly female, White, and privately insured, with a mean age of 49 years and mean BMI of 36 kg/m2. Most prescriptions were written by primary care providers. Among survey respondents in Phase II, 90.1% reported successfully filling their initial prescription and 80.5% remained on treatment. Among the 512 respondents who reported discontinued treatment, the most common reasons were insurance coverage discontinuation (37.7%), high medication costs (20.3%), and side effects (27.1%). Although 88.0% of respondents reported receiving medication-related instructions, only 27.0% reported receiving a referral to an additional health service, most commonly nutrition counseling. Patients prescribed contemporary anti-obesity medications were predominantly female, White, and privately insured. Financial barriers were the main reasons for treatment discontinuation, and potentially important referrals to nutrition and behavioral services were infrequent. These findings provide important real-world insights into the implementation of anti-obesity pharmacotherapy and identify leverage points for improving access, continued use, and multidisciplinary obesity treatment.

title: Long-Term Clinical Outcomes and Real-World Effectiveness of Tirzepatide in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Obesity is a chronic, progressive, and relapsing disease associated with substantial morbidity, premature mortality, and increased healthcare utilisation. Although lifestyle modification remains the cornerstone of management, long-term weight-loss maintenance is challenging. Tirzepatide, a once-weekly dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, has demonstrated substantial weight-loss efficacy, but its long-term clinical outcomes have not been comprehensively synthesised. A systematic search of Ovid MEDLINE ALL, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) was conducted from database inception to June 30, 2026. Eligible studies included Phase III randomised controlled trials, randomised withdrawal trials, long-term extension studies, prespecified secondary analyses reporting unique outcomes, and real-world observational studies. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) and Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tools. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively in accordance with the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines. Twenty-six publications representing 11 independent parent studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising eight Phase III randomised controlled trials, one long-term extension study, two real-world observational cohort studies, and 15 prespecified secondary analyses. Tirzepatide consistently produced substantial, dose-dependent, and durable weight reduction, with mean weight loss approaching 21% after 72 weeks. Continued therapy maintained weight loss, whereas treatment discontinuation resulted in progressive weight regain. Tirzepatide also improved cardiometabolic risk factors, body composition, physical functioning, and health-related quality of life. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common and were generally mild to moderate. Real-world studies demonstrated effectiveness and safety comparable to those observed in randomised clinical trials. Current evidence indicates that tirzepatide provides durable weight reduction and broad cardiometabolic benefits in adults with overweight or obesity. Sustained treatment is important for maintaining these benefits, while additional long-term studies are needed to evaluate treatment persistence, cardiovascular outcomes, comparative effectiveness, and long-term safety across diverse populations.

title: Can obesity pharmacotherapy modify osteoarthritis? Interpreting pain relief, weight-loss quality, and structural outcomes.
abstract: To evaluate the emerging role of obesity pharmacotherapies, particularly glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and multi-agonists, in osteoarthritis (OA) management, by examining the interpretation of pain outcomes, potential structural joint effects, the importance of weight-loss quality, implications for time to total joint replacement (TJR), and the patient populations most likely to benefit from current obesity pharmacotherapies. We conducted a narrative review of clinical and basic science literature examining the relationships between obesity, OA, and weight loss, with a particular focus on GLP-1 therapies and emerging obesity medications. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, translational investigations, and regulatory guidance documents was reviewed with emphasis on pain outcomes, structural joint effects, and factors influencing progression to TJR. Recent randomized controlled trials, primarily involving patients with OA and class III obesity (body mass index >40), demonstrate substantial pain reduction following obesity pharmacotherapy. However, interpretation of these benefits is complicated by obesity-associated pain, multimorbidity, and limitations of patient-reported outcomes such as WOMAC. Current evidence supports symptomatic improvement associated with weight loss, but whether obesity pharmacotherapies directly modify OA-related pain pathways or slow structural progression remains unknown. Moreover, the quality of weight loss may be important, as reductions in fat mass may be accompanied by bone loss and reduced muscle mass. Patients at heightened risk of structural deterioration, such as sarcopenia or elevated bone resorption, may be particularly vulnerable to these effects. Emerging concepts such as clinical obesity further highlight the biological heterogeneity of OA populations and suggest that treatment responses may differ considerably between patients. In the absence of evidence demonstrating direct joint structural modification, obesity pharmacotherapies cannot currently be considered disease-modifying OA treatments. Nonetheless, they may set a new benchmark for pain management in selected OA patients living with obesity. Because weight loss may not necessarily translate to structural benefit despite symptomatic improvement, pain should not serve as a stand-alone outcome in OA-obesity trials. Future studies should evaluate structural outcomes, weight-loss quality, and patient heterogeneity to ensure that obesity therapies deliver sustained symptomatic benefits in OA without compromising musculoskeletal health.

title: Exit Interviews Examining Patient Experiences with Tirzepatide and Dulaglutide for Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes in the SURPASS-CVOT Trial.
journal: Diabetes therapy : research, treatment and education of diabetes and related disorders
abstract: Qualitative exit interviews with people who recently completed a clinical trial can provide in-depth insights into their treatment experience and the benefits they consider most meaningful. The purpose of this exit interview study was to examine the impact of long-term treatment with dulaglutide and tirzepatide from the perspective of patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Interviews were conducted after participants completed treatment with either dulaglutide or tirzepatide in the multiyear SURPASS-CVOT clinical trial. Interviews were conducted by telephone or web-based conference using a semi-structured interview guide. The interviews were transcribed and analyzed following a content analysis approach. In total, 147 people were invited to participate in exit interviews across 10 US trial sites. A total of 74 participants were interviewed (63.5% male; mean age = 68.9 years), including 31 treated with dulaglutide and 43 treated with tirzepatide. Participants reported treatment benefits during the trial, such as improved glycemic control (97.3%), weight reduction (91.9%), reduced appetite (78.4%), improved diet and eating habits (64.9%), increased energy (56.8%), and decreased desire for unhealthy food (41.9%). Some also noted improvement in conditions other than T2D, including joint pain/osteoarthritis (18.9%) and sleep apnea (8.1%). Nearly all participants said these treatment-related changes were meaningful. Participants described improvements in quality of life and daily activities associated with treatment. The most commonly reported adverse event was nausea (28.4%). Most participants said they would be very likely (77.0%) or likely (16.2%) to recommend their treatment to others. Exit interview results indicate that self-reported treatment benefits were important to people who received long-term treatment with dulaglutide or tirzepatide.

title: Redefining weight management after liver transplantation with glucagon-like peptide one and gastric inhibitory polypeptide receptor agonists.
abstract: Obesity is a challenging complication that many liver transplant recipients face. Liver transplantation is the sole life-saving procedure in many end-stage liver diseases, but the underlying pathology, in addition to some immunosuppressive regimens, may worsen the metabolic status of many patients. A comprehensive management plan to prevent further metabolic complications, like metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, chronic renal dysfunction, and diabetes, is essential to obtain a favourable prognosis and a better quality of life. glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonists have been approved for long-term weight management by the United States Food and Drug Administration and other regulatory authorities. While this pharmacotherapeutic intervention revolutionised obesity management, it comes with many limitations.
